problem: Speech emotion labels are scarce and recordings are sensitive, making centralized collection and fully supervised training difficult.
contribution: An attention-based speech model combines federated self-training with a client-specific pseudo-label confidence schedule to use local labeled and unlabeled audio.
reading_guide: Compare equal label budgets within each partition, and keep unseen-speaker evaluation separate from evaluation with overlapping speakers.

diagram.title: Federated emotion learning
diagram.description: The server sends global weights to participating clients. Each client represents its local audio with an attention CNN, jointly trains with labels and accepted pseudo-labels, and returns parameters for aggregation.

stages.title: Broadcast weights
stages.detail: Send shared model parameters to the clients selected for a round.

stages.title: Attend to speech
stages.detail: Process local log-mel inputs with spectral, temporal and channel attention.

stages.title: Local self-training
stages.detail: Combine known labels with pseudo-labels passing a confidence threshold tied to round progress and participation.

stages.title: Federated averaging
stages.detail: Aggregate local model parameters and distribute the next global model.

diagram.footnote: The cycle repeats with aggregated weights. Raw audio stays local, but the study provides no formal differential-privacy guarantee or attack-resistance evaluation.

results.title: Unlabeled speech helps with 10% labels
results.question: Does self-training improve the same local model under each tested partition?
results.context: IEMOCAP improvised subset; neutral, happy, sad and angry. Mean unweighted accuracy (UA, %) over five runs per split; higher is better; no dispersion reported. Random partitions use 10 clients and per-speaker partitions use 8.
results.interpretation: Self-training improves all four equal-label comparisons, while remaining below the corresponding fully labeled federated reference.
results.caveat: Unseen-speaker results use leave-one-session-out evaluation; overlapping-speaker results use 80:20 splits with five-fold cross-validation. The latter is an easier generalization setting.

results.title: Centralized and federated references
results.question: How does moving the attention model to federated training affect the supervised reference?
results.context: Same four-emotion IEMOCAP subset; fully supervised random partitions. Mean UA (%), higher is better. The paper’s federated model uses 10 clients, 100 rounds, 80% participation and one local epoch; no dispersion reported.
results.interpretation: The same proposed architecture loses 2.06 UA points in unseen-speaker evaluation and 4.26 points with overlapping speakers when trained federatively.
results.caveat: The CNN Transformer is a cited literature reference, not an ablation of the proposed architecture. Centralized and federated results should be compared within each speaker protocol.

evaluation.label: Data
evaluation.value: IEMOCAP improvised speech only, four emotion categories; 16 kHz audio and two-second segments in the method text.

evaluation.label: Models
evaluation.value: Four-block convolutional model with spectral, temporal and channel attention; predictions averaged across non-overlapping utterance segments.

evaluation.label: Compared with
evaluation.value: Supervised FedAvg using the identical 10% labeled subset, fully labeled FedAvg, and centralized attention-based SER references.

evaluation.label: Protocol
evaluation.value: Flower simulation; leave-one-session-out for unseen speakers and five-fold 80:20 splits for overlapping speakers; random versus per-speaker client partitions.

limitations: Evidence is limited to one dataset’s improvised subset and four emotions; cross-language, cross-corpus and natural deployment generalization are untested.
Keeping recordings on devices reduces raw-data sharing but does not establish differential privacy or resistance to information leakage through updates.
The comparison reports means without dispersion, and per-speaker and random partitions also differ in client count.
The work simulates clients and does not provide real-device training energy or latency measurements.
takeaways: Unlabeled clips improve all four tested 10%-label federated settings, but do not fully close the gap to using all labels.
Separating speakers between training and testing is essential when assessing generalization to new users.
Data locality is a concrete system property; formal privacy protection requires evidence beyond this evaluation.
